tagline: Yeast cocultures that produce four plant specialized metabolites from sakura and tea - sakuranetin, quercetin, EGCG and L-theanine - without the plant
summary: ASIJ-Tokyo engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae to make four plant specialized metabolites tied to Japanese culture: sakuranetin, quercetin, EGCG and L-theanine. Rather than one overloaded strain, they split pathways across cocultured strains at optimised ratios (7:3 for sakuranetin and quercetin, 5:3:2 for the three-strain EGCG system), with every enzyme cassette behind a GAL promoter and a constitutive pTEF1 fluorescent reporter so strain ratios can be verified before induction. Their education portfolio is unusually broad for a high-school team and explicitly gap-driven: each activity was created to fill a named gap they had identified. They contributed 34 new parts, a no-HPLC semi-quantitative screening workflow and a low-cost DIY bioreactor with full build instructions, all aimed at other resource-limited high-school teams.

dry.frameworks: Stakeholder analysis structured into three domains (agricultural supply, health and consumer needs, production and commercial viability); Duke iGEM's Risk and Research Ethics Assessment tool used as an external bioethics compliance check.
dry.dataviz: Stakeholder map figure grouping identified issues and stakeholders into the three domains; coculture architecture diagrams.
dry.datascience: A semi-quantitative screening workflow designed specifically for teams without HPLC access, published as a contribution. In-silico modelling of a proposed active-transport system was explored with guidance from a Johns Hopkins biomedical engineering student, then explicitly abandoned because without HPLC the team could not measure intra- versus extracellular compound concentrations to validate it - a documented negative result.
dry.software: Village 茶(Sa)kura: a free Animal Crossing-style educational game built in Unity and coded in C# over two years with the Japanese technology entertainment company ABAL Inc. Players receive villager requests (for example 'bring me anti-inflammatory sakura cream'), scavenge ingredients in the Sakura Forest, read recipes at crafting stations, synthesise items in in-game labs and return them, with up to 10 encoded pathways; published free on itch.io with a game manual. Also a memory card game, a 'What is?' YouTube explainer series, and The Catalyst: Science & Curiosity, a student science news/publication website.

good.publicEngagement: ASIJ-Tokyo opened its education work with a diagnostic question - who is not yet part of the synthetic biology conversation - and then built one artefact per identified gap, which makes the portfolio unusually legible. Gap: low public awareness of sakura's health properties, addressed by an Earth Day booth (22 April 2025 and 2026) where elementary, middle and high school students painted flower pots and took home sakura seeds while being briefed on anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, reaching 70+ participants each year, plus a Sakura & Matcha Goodies recipe book whose recipes each carry a 'the science behind' blurb. Gap: almost no synthetic biology video content pitched at high school level, addressed by a 'What is?' YouTube series running since 2023 covering bioethics, cellular transport, yeast in synthetic biology, metabolic engineering, genetic switches, cocultures, biosensors and cellular fluorescence, deliberately sequenced so concepts build on each other. Gap: little attention to memory degradation in Japan's ageing population, addressed by a memory card game run at a senior home on 13 October 2026, using six cards depicting cluttered domestic interiors with recall questions (colour of the couch, number of pencils) across repeated rounds individually and in groups of 2-3; the team was scrupulous about its limits, stating plainly that this was a small pilot and not a clinical study, and left the game with the facility and its nurses as a low-pressure cognitive exercise. Gap: no easy way for teachers outside iGEM or biology to run these activities, addressed by a free downloadable workbook of seven tested lesson plans covering DNA, natural pigment, cell modelling, chromatography, biomaterials and polymer creation, refined so that the labs connect into a holistic overview, plus The Catalyst: Science & Curiosity, a newspaper-style website that also acts as a publication platform where any secondary school student can publish science writing from 300-word pieces to 20-page experimental reports. The flagship format is Village 茶(Sa)kura, an Animal Crossing-style Unity/C# game co-developed over two years with ABAL Inc., a Japanese technology entertainment company, iterated against industry-expert feedback and published free on itch.io with a manual. Direct teaching reached a wide spread of ages: a four-year-running CRISPR-Cas9 and gel electrophoresis lab for 8th graders built into their sickle cell anaemia unit (13-14 May 2025 and 12-13 May 2026, including why researchers target the BCL11A enhancer rather than the mutation itself); DNA extraction workshops for over 30 students at Tokyo Bay International School and Montessori School Tokyo in Azabu (31 March and 22 July 2026); the same experiment with bananas for 80+ children aged 5-10 daily at the school's Summer Day Camp, deliberately reaching local and non-international-school children; a 60+ child booth with leaf-rubbing and plant-engineering discussion at Aoyama Gakuin's Global Day (21 October 2025), tied to the UN SDGs and to English-language learning; a Winterfest campus-wide CSI escape-room-style DNA mystery (4 December 2025) with three stations - DNA matching to eliminate suspects, leaf-morphology comparison to locate the crime scene, and gel electrophoresis to identify the culprit; a Community Health Fair obstacle-course race (11 April 2025) where participants acted as skin cells carrying sakuranetin past crawl-space 'constricted blood vessels' and hurdle 'blockages' on a two-minute timer; and Back to School Night in 2025 and 2026, the 2026 edition adding a hands-on flower pipetting activity and recipe-book matcha cookies for 100+ parents, students and teachers. Evidence of iteration is explicit and honest: PCR was cut from the 8th grade lab because crucial steps ran out of time, lesson plans were reworked so activities connect, pipetting was added to Back to School Night, and the team states openly that it did not systematically record feedback this year and therefore added a feedback page to the workbook so teachers who use it can report back. Collaboration was a deliberate education strategy in its own right: activities were created or joined with eight teams across eight countries (Duke, Maastricht, Manipal, Concordia, Ruhr University Bochum, St Stephen's College Hong Kong, Patras, KCIS Xiugang) plus the iGEM Community Blackboard - contributing a scent to Manipal's Scents of the World, an abstract to Maastricht's peer-reviewed MSP Vector journal, a Pokemon-style card to RUBochum's Trading Card Project, a Japanese translation of HKSSC's food-waste comic, and both of their games to Patras's downloadable game gallery.
good.ihp: Four stakeholder engagements reshaped the project, each with a recorded design consequence. Tea producer Masahiro Okutomi of Sayama-cha Okutomien (10 April 2026) explained that overseas matcha orders have risen sharply while new tea plants take at least five years to mature and processing equipment three years to arrive, and that L-theanine is what gives matcha much of its quality - so extracting it from leaves for supplements would leave farmers with a degraded product. This directly strengthened the decision to produce L-theanine in yeast rather than extract it, and reframed the team's positioning from replacement to 'an extra source that works beside farms'. He also noted Japanese companies market catechins like EGCG while consumers do not know what L-theanine does, which changed the team's communication plan to explain each compound separately starting with L-theanine. Yukari Kawahito of Sakura Science Beauty (May 2026) introduced transdermal patches as a delivery format the team had not considered and opened a second business route of selling compounds to companies with existing formulation capability. Vikki Adams (Johns Hopkins) advised on an in-silico active-transport model that was ultimately dropped for lack of HPLC validation. A visit to the six-generation family-run Maruichi Mizuno Tea Farm in Shizuoka (16 June 2026) showed how the farm covers plants with sheets, harvests three times a year, processes its own hojicha and sencha and is now seeking matcha manufacturers to benefit from the boom - confirming producers already market L-theanine and EGCG benefits while demand for fermentation-derived ingredients remains untested. The visit was filmed as a vlog.
good.realWorld: The project's framing is a supply constraint, not a novelty: sakura-flavoured products appear across Japanese supermarkets every spring and vanish by May because the raw material does, sakuranetin being bound to one of the shortest harvest windows in agriculture, while tea faces the opposite problem of a demand boom farms cannot meet. Contributions were deliberately designed for resource-limited high-school teams: a reusable coculture architecture where a future team can keep Strain N unchanged and only build its own downstream strain, 34 new Registry parts, a semi-quantitative screening workflow usable without HPLC, and a low-cost DIY bioreactor with full build instructions. The team hosted six students from St Mary's International School to build a biosensor, gained HPLC access through a bioanalytical chemistry professor at International Christian University, and will give an opening keynote alongside university professors at ASIJ's first semi-annual science fair on 14 November 2026 to roughly 100 students and teachers.

gemsTakeaway: Start from a written list of named gaps (which audience, which missing resource) and build exactly one artefact per gap, then package the reusable ones - a seven-lesson tested workbook with a built-in feedback page, a free game, a sequenced video series - so teachers outside synthetic biology can run them without you.
